question: Let \(n\) be the least positive integer greater than \(1000\) for which \[ \begin{gathered} \gcd(63,n+120)=21\\ \text{and}\\ \gcd(n+63,120)=60. \end{gathered} \] What is the sum of the digits of \(n?\)
solution:
Adding \(63\) to \(n+120\) and adding \(120\) to \(n+63\) produce the same expression, \(n+183\). This combines the two divisibility conditions neatly.

Adding a multiple of one number to the other does not change their common divisors. Therefore, setting \(m=n+183\), the given conditions become
\[
\gcd(63,m)=21,
\qquad
\gcd(m,120)=60.
\]
In particular, \(m\) is divisible by both \(21\) and \(60\), so it is divisible by their least common multiple, \(420\). Write
\[
m=420k
\]
for a positive integer \(k\).

We must still enforce the exact greatest common divisors. Since
\[
63=21\cdot3,
\qquad
m=21\cdot20k,
\]
the first gcd equals \(21\) exactly when \(20k\) is not divisible by \(3\), or equivalently when \(k\) is not divisible by \(3\).

Likewise,
\[
120=60\cdot2,
\qquad
m=60\cdot7k,
\]
so the second gcd equals \(60\) exactly when \(7k\) is odd, or equivalently when \(k\) is odd.

The restriction \(n>1000\) gives
\[
420k=n+183>1183,
\]
so \(k\geq3\). The value \(3\) is excluded because it is divisible by \(3\), and \(4\) is excluded because it is even. The next value, \(k=5\), satisfies both requirements. Since \(n=420k-183\) increases with \(k\), this gives the least possible \(n\):
\[
n=420\cdot5-183=1917.
\]
Its digit sum is
\[
1+9+1+7=\boxed{18},
\]
choice \(\mathrm{C}\).

solutionMethods.explanation:
The second gcd condition says that \(n+63\) is an odd multiple of \(60\). Using this exact restriction first avoids candidates whose gcd would be \(120\).

Indeed, because \(120=2\cdot60\), we can write
\[
n+63=60(2q+1),
\qquad
n=120q-3
\]
for an integer \(q\). The condition \(n>1000\) forces \(q\geq9\).

The first gcd condition requires \(21\mid n+120\). Substituting our expression for \(n\), this means
\[
21\mid120q+117=3(40q+39),
\]
so \(7\mid40q+39\). To find the possible values of \(q\), observe that
\[
40q+39=7(6q+5)-2(q-2).
\]
Thus \(7\mid2(q-2)\). Since \(7\) and \(2\) have no common factor, \(q-2\) must be divisible by \(7\). The possible values with \(q\geq9\) are therefore
\[
q=9,16,23,\ldots.
\]

For \(q=9\), we obtain \(n=1077\), but
\[
n+120=1197=63\cdot19,
\]
so the first gcd is \(63\), which fails.

The next candidate, \(q=16\), gives \(n=1917\). Here
\[
n+120=2037=21\cdot97,
\qquad
n+63=1980=60\cdot33.
\]
Because \(97\) is not divisible by \(3\) and \(33\) is odd, the gcds are exactly \(21\) and \(60\). These candidates were considered in increasing order, so \(1917\) is the least valid integer above \(1000\).

The requested digit sum is
\[
1+9+1+7=\boxed{18},
\]
choice \(\mathrm{C}\).
